source.title: Evening Screen Light and Falling Asleep
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined whether the brightness and color of a tablet screen used in the evening affect how long it takes people to fall asleep that night.

Ninety-six students from two community colleges in Arizona were recruited through flyers posted on campus and a message sent to students who had signed up for a research email list. Students were not eligible if they had been diagnosed with a sleep disorder, took any medication to help them sleep, or had worked a night shift in the past month. Of the 117 students who completed the online screening survey, 21 were not eligible or could not attend all four nights. Each participant received a $40 gift card after the final night of the study.

Participants ranged in age from 18 to 26 years (mean age = 20.4 years, standard deviation = 1.9 years). The sample was 58% women, 41% men, and 1% nonbinary. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 44% Hispanic/Latino/a, 31% White, 12% Black/African American, 8% Asian/Asian American, and 5% multiracial. Most participants (71%) also held a part-time job. For one week before the study, each participant kept a written sleep diary; the average bedtime they reported was 12:10 a.m.

Before any data were collected, the study plan was reviewed and approved by the colleges' institutional review board. At an orientation session, a researcher explained the procedures, including that participants would spend four nights in a sleep laboratory and would wear a wrist monitor while they slept. Each participant then read and signed a consent form. Participants were told that they could stop taking part at any time and would still receive the gift card. Each participant was given an ID number, and only ID numbers appeared on the data files, which were stored on a password-protected computer.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions:
- Bright screen condition: participants read on a tablet set to full brightness with the standard white display.
- Dim screen condition: participants read on the same model of tablet set to its lowest brightness with a warm, amber-colored filter turned on.

The first night in the laboratory was an adjustment night, and no data from it were used. On each of the next three nights, participants arrived at 8:30 p.m. and completed a 10-minute questionnaire about their caffeine use and activities that day. From 9:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m., each participant sat alone in a private bedroom and read the same novel on their assigned tablet. Phones were collected at the door. The overhead lights in each room were kept dim and were the same in both conditions, and each room was kept at 68°F. A research assistant checked on each participant through an intercom at 10:00 p.m. The novel was chosen because none of the participants had read it before and its plot had nothing to do with sleep.

At 10:45 p.m., participants gave a small saliva sample, which was later tested for melatonin. Lights went out at 11:00 p.m. Sleep onset latency was measured as the number of minutes between lights-out and the first time the wrist monitor recorded 10 minutes in a row of sleep. The monitor also recorded total sleep time. Participants were woken at 7:00 a.m. and completed a 5-minute reaction-time test on a computer, pressing a key as soon as a dot appeared on the screen.

Two participants in the bright screen condition left the study after the adjustment night for reasons unrelated to the study, and their data were not used. For each remaining participant, the researchers averaged the measures across the three study nights. The mean results for each condition are shown in the table.

Table: Mean Results for Each Screen Condition
| Measure | Bright screen | Dim screen |
| Sleep onset latency (minutes) | 31.6 | 18.2 |
| Melatonin at 10:45 p.m. (picograms per milliliter) | 9.4 | 15.1 |
| Total sleep time (hours and minutes) | 6 h 41 min | 7 h 02 min |
| Morning reaction time (milliseconds) | 312 | 305 |

Participants in the bright screen condition took significantly longer to fall asleep than participants in the dim screen condition (p < .001). Their melatonin levels before lights-out were also significantly lower (p = .002). The differences in total sleep time and in morning reaction time were not statistically significant.

Participants' answers on the caffeine questionnaire did not differ between the two conditions. The researchers noted that the study lasted only three nights and took place in a laboratory, where participants could not use their phones or follow their usual bedtime routines.

items.title: Caffeine Dose and Reaction Time

source.title: Caffeine Dose and Reaction Time
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined whether the amount of caffeine a person consumes affects how quickly they respond to a simple visual signal.

Participants were 120 adults recruited through an online ad posted by a university hospital in Ohio. To take part, adults had to drink no more than two caffeinated drinks a day, have no heart problems, and not be pregnant. Of the 151 adults who filled out the online screening form, 31 did not meet these requirements or could not attend a morning session. Participants were paid $30 for one 3-hour session, and parking was provided.

Participants ranged in age from 21 to 45 years (mean age = 29.8 years, standard deviation = 6.2 years). The sample was 54% women and 46% men. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 62% White, 18% Black/African American, 11% Asian/Asian American, 6% Hispanic/Latino/a, and 3% multiracial. About half of the participants (48%) worked full-time, and 31% were students. On the screening form, participants reported drinking an average of 1.2 caffeinated drinks per day, most often coffee.

The hospital's ethics board approved the study before it began. When participants arrived, a nurse checked their blood pressure, and a researcher explained that they would drink a beverage that might contain caffeine and then complete computer tasks. Participants signed a consent form, and they were told that they could end the session at any time and would still be paid.

Participants were asked not to eat or drink anything with caffeine for 24 hours before the session, and all sessions began at 8:00 a.m. Participants were given a plain bagel and water when they arrived so that no one would be tested on an empty stomach. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of three groups:
- No caffeine group: a drink containing 0 milligrams of caffeine.
- Low dose group: a drink containing 100 milligrams of caffeine, about the amount in one cup of coffee.
- High dose group: a drink containing 300 milligrams of caffeine.

All three drinks were 350 milliliters of the same lemon-flavored beverage and looked and tasted the same. Participants were asked to finish the drink within 5 minutes. Neither the participants nor the researcher running the session knew which drink a participant received.

After drinking the beverage, participants waited 45 minutes in a quiet room, where they could read magazines. They then sat at a computer in a small testing room with the lights dimmed and the door closed and completed a 10-minute reaction-time task. Before the real trials began, each participant completed 10 practice trials, which were not counted. A gray square appeared in the center of a computer screen at random intervals, and participants pressed the space bar as quickly as possible each time it appeared. Reaction time was measured as the average number of milliseconds between the square appearing and the key press, across 60 trials. Participants also rated how alert they felt from 1 (very sleepy) to 7 (very alert) and completed a short word puzzle that was not scored for this study.

At the end of the session, the nurse checked blood pressure again, and each participant was told which drink they had received. Participants who had received caffeine were reminded that it could make it harder to fall asleep that night if they drank more later in the day.

Three participants in the high dose group stopped the session early because they felt jittery, and their data were not used. The results for the remaining participants are shown in the table.

Table: Mean Results for Each Group
| Measure | No caffeine | Low dose | High dose |
| Reaction time (milliseconds) | 338 | 305 | 301 |
| Alertness rating (1 to 7) | 3.9 | 5.1 | 5.4 |
| Participants who reported feeling jittery | 3% | 10% | 37% |

Both caffeine groups had significantly faster reaction times than the no caffeine group (p < .01). The difference between the low dose and high dose groups was not statistically significant. Both caffeine groups also rated themselves as significantly more alert than the no caffeine group.

Blood pressure rose slightly more in the high dose group than in the other groups, but no participant's blood pressure reached an unsafe level. The researchers noted that the participants were light caffeine users and that the results might differ for people who drink caffeine every day.

source.title: Weekly Exercise and Depressive Symptoms in Teens
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined the relationship between how much high school students exercise and how many symptoms of depression they report.

Participants were 640 students in grades 9 through 12 at six public high schools in North Carolina. The schools were chosen because their principals agreed to take part. All students in the selected classes were invited, and 71% of those invited took part. Students who were absent on the day of the survey were not given a second chance to take it. Each participant was entered into a drawing for one of twenty $25 gift cards.

Participants ranged in age from 14 to 18 years (mean age = 15.9 years, standard deviation = 1.1 years). The sample was 52% girls, 46% boys, and 2% another gender identity. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 48% White, 27% Black/African American, 15% Hispanic/Latino/a, 5% Asian/Asian American, and 5% multiracial. Thirty-eight percent of participants played on at least one school sports team, and 41% received free or reduced-price school lunch. Two of the six schools were in rural areas, three in suburbs, and one in a city.

The study was approved by a university's institutional review board and by the school district. Parents received a letter describing the study and returned a signed form if they agreed to let their child take part. Students also signed an assent form. Students were told that they could skip any question or stop at any time, and that their teachers would never see their answers. Surveys were labeled with code numbers instead of names.

Students completed the survey on school laptops during a homeroom period, which took about 25 minutes. A research assistant, not the teacher, handed out the laptops and answered questions. Students who did not take part read silently at their desks. Exercise was measured with the question "In the past 7 days, on how many days were you physically active for a total of at least 60 minutes per day?" Answers ranged from 0 to 7 days. Depressive symptoms were measured with a 20-item questionnaire asking how often in the past week students had felt sad, hopeless, tired, or uninterested in things they usually enjoy. Scores ranged from 0 to 60, with higher scores meaning more symptoms.

Before the main study, the researchers tested the exercise question with a separate group of 40 students who also wore step-counting watches for a week; students who reported more active days also took more steps. The survey also asked about hours of sleep on school nights, hours of screen time per day, and how many close friends the student had. It also asked whether the student had a job and how they got to school (walking, biking, bus, or car). Any student whose depression score was 40 or higher received a private message with information about the school counselor and a free support line.

The researchers chose to survey students in late October, after the start of the school year but before winter break, so that holidays and final exams would not affect students' answers. All six schools completed the survey within the same two weeks, and each school received a short report of its overall results, with no information about individual students.

Table: Mean Depressive Symptom Score by Days of Exercise per Week
| Days of exercise in the past week | Percent of students | Mean depressive symptom score (0 to 60) |
| 0 to 1 days | 22% | 24.6 |
| 2 to 4 days | 47% | 17.9 |
| 5 to 7 days | 31% | 12.3 |

Days of exercise were negatively correlated with depressive symptom scores (r = -.41, p < .001). Students who exercised on more days tended to report fewer symptoms of depression. Hours of sleep were also negatively correlated with depressive symptoms (r = -.33), and hours of screen time were positively correlated with depressive symptoms (r = .22).

Girls reported slightly higher depressive symptom scores than boys on average (19.4 vs. 16.2), and boys reported more days of exercise. Students who walked or biked to school did not differ from other students in depressive symptoms. The researchers noted that students who play sports may also spend more time with friends and coaches, and that students who feel depressed may have less energy to exercise.

Students who feel depressed may have less energy to exercise, or a third variable like sleep or time with friends on sports teams could explain both.

items.title: Exposure Therapy for Fear of Spiders

A.trapHint: There were 64 participants randomly assigned to exposure or a waiting list, so this is an experiment, not a case study of one person.

Gives how this study measured it (steps out of 12 toward the spider in the approach test)

source.title: Exposure Therapy for Fear of Spiders
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study tested whether a single long session of exposure therapy reduces fear and avoidance in adults with an intense fear of spiders.

Participants were recruited through ads on a university website and in local newspapers in Oregon. Adults who responded completed a phone interview with a clinical psychologist, and those who met the criteria for a specific phobia of spiders were invited to take part. People who were receiving other treatment for anxiety, or who had a heart condition, were not eligible. Of the 97 adults who completed the phone interview, 71 met the criteria, and 7 of those decided not to take part.

The final sample was 64 adults aged 19 to 58 years (mean age = 31.4 years, standard deviation = 9.7 years). The sample was 81% women and 19% men. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 77% White, 9% Asian/Asian American, 8% Hispanic/Latino/a, 3% Black/African American, and 3% multiracial. Most participants (72%) said their fear had started before age 10, and many said they checked rooms for spiders before entering them. Participants did not receive payment, but those in the waiting list group were offered free treatment after the study ended.

The university's institutional review board approved the study. At the first visit, a psychologist explained that participants might be asked to be near or touch a live spider, which could cause strong fear. Participants signed a consent form. They were told that they could stop any task, or leave the study, at any time.

Before treatment, each participant completed a behavioral approach test. A live, harmless house spider sat in a covered glass tank at the far end of a 6-meter hallway. Participants were asked to walk toward the tank and do as many of 12 steps as they could, such as standing 1 meter from the tank, removing the lid, and letting the spider walk on a gloved hand. Avoidance was measured as the number of steps completed, from 0 to 12. At each step, participants also rated their fear from 0 (no fear) to 100 (the most fear imaginable), and the highest rating was recorded. They then filled out a questionnaire about their history of other fears and how much the fear affected their daily life, such as avoiding camping or basements. The test took about 15 minutes, and a researcher stood beside the participant the whole time.

Participants who completed all 12 steps before treatment would not have been included, but none did. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of two groups:
1. Exposure group: one 3-hour session with a therapist. The participant gradually moved closer to spiders of increasing size, staying with each step until their fear dropped by about half. The therapist first showed each step, such as holding a spider in a cup, and then helped the participant try it. Sessions took place in a quiet office with a window, and participants could take short breaks for water.
2. Waiting list group: no treatment during the study.

One week later, every participant completed the behavioral approach test again with a different spider of about the same size. Participants in the exposure group were also asked to look at photos of spiders for 10 minutes a day during that week, and most said they had done so on at least 5 days. The researcher who ran the test did not know which group each participant was in. After the test, participants also rated how confident they felt that they could handle seeing a spider at home, from 0 (not at all confident) to 10 (completely confident).

Table: Mean Results Before and One Week After Treatment
| Group | Steps completed before | Steps completed after | Fear rating before (0 to 100) | Fear rating after (0 to 100) |
| Exposure | 3.1 | 10.4 | 86 | 31 |
| Waiting list | 3.3 | 3.8 | 84 | 80 |

One week after treatment, participants in the exposure group completed significantly more steps and reported significantly less fear than participants in the waiting list group (p < .001). Twenty-two of the 32 participants in the exposure group (69%) completed all 12 steps, compared with none in the waiting list group.

Two participants in the exposure group stopped the session early, and their after-treatment scores were included in the analysis. Confidence ratings rose from an average of 2.2 to 7.6 in the exposure group and stayed near 2 in the waiting list group. The researchers noted that the study did not test whether the improvement lasted beyond one week, and that all of the therapists had years of experience treating phobias.

source.title: Exam Stress and Catching a Cold
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined whether college students who report more stress during final exams are more likely to report cold symptoms in the weeks around exams.

Participants were 212 undergraduate students at a private university in Pennsylvania. Students were recruited through an email sent to all students living in campus housing. They received course credit or $20 for taking part. Of the 260 students who replied to the email, 48 were not included because they had a long-term illness, took medication that affects the immune system, or were studying abroad that semester.

Participants ranged in age from 18 to 24 years (mean age = 20.1 years, standard deviation = 1.4 years). The sample was 57% women and 43% men. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 59% White, 16% Asian/Asian American, 12% Hispanic/Latino/a, 9% Black/African American, and 4% multiracial. Eighty-four percent of participants lived in a residence hall with a roommate, and the rest lived alone. About a third of participants (34%) also had a part-time job on campus.

The university's institutional review board approved the study. Students read an online consent page explaining that they would answer short surveys on their phones for four weeks, and they clicked a button to agree. The consent page said that students could stop at any time, and that their answers would be stored without their names.

The study began in late November. Two weeks before final exams, students completed the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale, which asks how often in the past month they felt nervous and stressed or unable to handle everything they had to do. Scores range from 0 to 40, with higher scores meaning more stress. Students also reported how many exams and papers they had due and how many hours per week they usually exercised. These first surveys took about 15 minutes and were completed online.

For the next four weeks, which included the two weeks of final exams, students received a text message each evening with a link to a short checklist. Cold symptoms were measured as the number of days on which a student reported at least two of the following: sneezing, a runny or stuffy nose, a sore throat, or a cough. Students also reported hours of sleep each night and whether they had gotten a flu shot that year. The checklist asked how many cups of coffee or energy drinks the student had that day, but the researchers did not use those answers in this report. A research assistant checked the responses each week and contacted any student who had missed three or more days in a row to ask whether they wanted to continue.

Each checklist took about 1 minute. If a student missed a day, a reminder was sent the next morning, but students could not fill in checklists for earlier days. Students who completed at least 24 of the 28 daily checklists were included in the analysis.

At the end of the four weeks, students answered a few questions about whether they had used any cold medicine and whether anyone they lived with had been sick. Students were then sent a summary explaining what the researchers were studying.

Of the 212 students, 188 completed enough checklists to be included. Stress scores were positively correlated with the number of days with cold symptoms (r = .36, p < .001). Students who reported more stress before exams tended to report more days with cold symptoms during the four weeks.

Table: Days with Cold Symptoms by Stress Level
| Stress score group | Number of students | Mean days with cold symptoms (out of 28) |
| Low (0 to 13) | 51 | 2.1 |
| Medium (14 to 26) | 94 | 4.6 |
| High (27 to 40) | 43 | 7.8 |

Average hours of sleep were negatively correlated with days of cold symptoms (r = -.29). Students with higher stress scores also slept fewer hours on average. Getting a flu shot was not related to the number of days with cold symptoms.

Students who said that a roommate had been sick also reported more days with cold symptoms. Exercise hours were not significantly related to days with cold symptoms. The number of exams and papers due was only weakly related to days with cold symptoms (r = .12). The researchers noted that cold symptoms were reported by the students and were not confirmed by a doctor, and that the study took place during winter, when colds are common on campus.

source.title: Virtual Reality Distraction During a Needle Procedure
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined whether playing a virtual reality game during a blood draw changes how much pain children report.

Participants were 156 children aged 8 to 14 who were having blood drawn for a routine test at an outpatient clinic of a children's hospital in Texas. Families were approached in the waiting room by a research assistant. Children who had a blood draw scheduled for a long-term illness, who had a history of seizures, or who had trouble seeing were not eligible. Of the 203 families approached, 47 declined, most often because they were in a hurry.

The children's mean age was 10.9 years (standard deviation = 1.8 years). The sample was 49% girls and 51% boys. The race/ethnicity of the children was reported by their parents as follows: 46% Hispanic/Latino/a, 28% White, 18% Black/African American, 5% Asian/Asian American, and 3% multiracial. Most children (68%) said they had had blood drawn at least once before. Each family received a $15 gift card.

The hospital's institutional review board approved the study. A research assistant explained the study to each parent, who signed a consent form, and to each child, who agreed in writing on a simple assent form. Families were told that they could stop at any time without any effect on the child's care.

Before the blood draw, each child rated how worried they felt about the needle on a scale from 0 (not worried) to 10 (very worried). Children were then randomly assigned to one of three conditions:
1. Virtual reality condition: the child wore a virtual reality headset and played an underwater game, in which they steered a submarine and collected glowing fish, starting 1 minute before the needle went in.
2. Tablet condition: the child watched a cartoon of their choice on a tablet held by a parent, starting at the same time.
3. Standard care condition: the child received the clinic's usual care, in which the nurse talked with the child and a parent could hold their hand.

Parents in all three conditions could stay in the room. Six nurses with at least 3 years of experience did all of the blood draws, and each nurse worked with children in all three conditions. The blood draws took an average of 4 minutes.

Within 1 minute after the needle was removed, a research assistant who had not been in the room asked the child to point to one of six faces on the Faces Pain Scale, ranging from a smiling face (0, no pain) to a crying face (10, the most pain possible). Pain was measured as the number under the face the child pointed to. Parents also rated how upset their child seemed during the draw, and the nurse recorded whether the needle had to be inserted more than once.

Before the study began, the research team tested the virtual reality game with 12 children who were not in the study to make sure that the headset fit children of different sizes and that the game was easy to learn in under a minute. The headsets were cleaned with wipes after every use. All blood draws took place between 8:00 a.m. and noon in the same two rooms, which had the same chairs, lighting, and pictures on the walls. After the study, each child was allowed to play the virtual reality game for 5 minutes, whatever condition they had been in.

Worry ratings before the blood draw did not differ significantly among the three conditions. Pain ratings after the draw are shown in the table.

Table: Mean Ratings for Each Condition
| Condition | Number of children | Worry before (0 to 10) | Pain rating (0 to 10) |
| Virtual reality | 52 | 5.4 | 2.3 |
| Tablet | 53 | 5.2 | 3.9 |
| Standard care | 51 | 5.6 | 5.6 |

Children in the virtual reality condition reported significantly less pain than children in the standard care condition (p < .001) and than children in the tablet condition (p = .01). Children in the tablet condition reported significantly less pain than those in standard care (p = .02). Parents also rated children in the virtual reality condition as less upset.

The needle had to be inserted more than once for 11 children, spread across all three conditions. Four children in the virtual reality condition said the headset made them feel a little dizzy, and one asked to remove it. The researchers noted that the nurses could see which condition each child was in.

A.trapHint: Participants were randomly assigned to what they drank and what they were told, so the researchers manipulated it: that makes it an experiment.

source.title: What You Think Is in Your Drink
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined whether believing you have had an energy drink changes how energetic you feel and how well you do on a timed math task, even when the drink has no caffeine.

Participants were 105 undergraduate students at a public university in Colorado who signed up through the psychology department's research website. The study was listed as "Drinks and Problem Solving." Students received 1 hour of course credit. Sessions were held between 1:00 and 4:00 p.m., and participants were asked not to have any caffeine after 9:00 a.m. on the day of their session. Six students who said they had had coffee that afternoon were rescheduled.

Participants ranged in age from 18 to 25 years (mean age = 19.7 years, standard deviation = 1.5 years). The sample was 60% women and 40% men. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 65% White, 17% Hispanic/Latino/a, 8% Asian/Asian American, 4% Black/African American, and 6% multiracial. On a screening survey, 44% said they drank an energy drink at least once a week. Students who reported heart problems or a bad reaction to caffeine were not eligible.

The university's institutional review board approved the study, including its use of deception. Participants were told that the study was about how drinks affect problem solving, that they might drink a beverage containing caffeine, and that they could leave at any time and still receive credit. They then signed a consent form.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions:
1. Energy drink condition: participants were told they were drinking an energy drink and received a drink with 160 milligrams of caffeine.
2. Placebo condition: participants were told they were drinking an energy drink but received the same drink with no caffeine.
3. Water condition: participants were told they were drinking flavored water and received the same drink with no caffeine.

All drinks were 250 milliliters, were the same color, and were served in a plain cup. For the energy drink and placebo conditions, the researcher poured the drink from a can with a well-known energy drink label. For the water condition, the drink was poured from a plain bottle.

After drinking, participants sat for 20 minutes in a small room with a desk and a window and filled out a questionnaire about their study habits, such as how many hours they studied each week and whether they listened to music while studying. The researcher left the room during this time. They then rated how energetic they felt on a scale from 1 (not at all energetic) to 10 (extremely energetic). Next, they had 5 minutes to solve as many two-digit multiplication problems as they could, such as 47 × 26, without a calculator. Math performance was measured as the number of problems answered correctly. Finally, participants guessed whether their drink had contained caffeine and rated how much they liked its taste.

To make sure the drinks tasted the same, the researchers first asked 20 different students to taste the caffeine and no-caffeine versions; they could not tell them apart better than chance. The same researcher, a graduate student, ran every session and read the same instructions from a script.

At the end of the session, the researcher explained the real purpose of the study, told each participant what their drink had actually contained, and explained why the study could not be described fully at the start.

Table: Mean Results for Each Condition
| Condition | Energy rating (1 to 10) | Math problems correct | Guessed the drink had caffeine |
| Energy drink | 7.2 | 14.8 | 89% |
| Placebo | 6.6 | 11.9 | 83% |
| Water | 4.3 | 11.4 | 9% |

Participants in the placebo condition rated themselves as significantly more energetic than participants in the water condition (p < .001), and their ratings were not significantly different from those in the energy drink condition. For math performance, the energy drink condition solved significantly more problems than both other conditions (p < .01), but the placebo and water conditions did not differ significantly.

Weekly energy drink users and nonusers showed the same pattern of results. Participants in the two caffeine-free conditions liked the taste of their drink about as much as participants in the energy drink condition. Four participants said during the debriefing that they had suspected the drink might not be what the label said, but their results were similar to everyone else's, so their data were kept. The researchers noted that the math task lasted only 5 minutes and that the energy rating was taken only once.

This indicates that people who believed they had an energy drink felt more energetic even though their drink had no caffeine, and the difference was unlikely to be due to chance.

The placebo condition rated their energy 6.6, almost as high as the energy drink condition (7.2) and much higher than the water condition (4.3), even though the placebo drink had no caffeine. That shows expectations alone made people feel more energetic. But the placebo condition solved about the same number of math problems as the water condition (11.9 vs. 11.4), so expectations changed how people felt, not how they performed.

items.title: Memory After Damage to the Hippocampus

A.trapHint: The researchers studied one man in depth and did not assign anyone to conditions; comparing him with 10 other men doesn't make it an experiment. It is a case study.

labels: Says it was the number of story details
Gives how this study measured it (details out of 25 repeated 30 minutes later)

source.title: Memory After Damage to the Hippocampus
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This report describes the memory of one man, called M.R. in this report, after an illness damaged the hippocampus on both sides of his brain.

M.R. is a 58-year-old right-handed man from Michigan who worked as an electrician for 31 years. Three years before this study, he developed a viral infection that caused swelling in his brain. Brain scans taken after he recovered showed damage to the hippocampus on both sides of his brain, with little damage to other areas. He has 12 years of education and lives with his wife, who helps him keep a daily calendar. Before his illness, he coached his grandson's baseball team and enjoyed fishing. Since the illness, he has not been able to return to work, and his wife reports that he often asks the same question several times in an hour. His speech, his vision, and his ability to walk were not affected, and his score on a standard intelligence test was in the average range.

For comparison, the researchers also tested 10 men with no history of brain injury who were similar to M.R. in age (mean age = 57.2 years, range = 52 to 63), years of education, and type of work. Comparison participants were recruited through a community center and were paid $50. M.R. was not paid, but his travel costs were covered.

The hospital's institutional review board approved the study. Because of his memory problems, the study was explained to both M.R. and his wife, and both signed consent forms. The researchers reminded M.R. at the start of each session that he could stop at any time. To protect his privacy, his name and the name of his hometown were not used in this report.

M.R. was tested in six sessions over 2 months, each lasting about 2 hours, in a quiet room at the hospital. The comparison participants each completed one session. Testing included the following tasks:
- Story recall: the researcher read aloud a short story containing 25 details, such as names, places, and events. Participants repeated as much of the story as they could right away (immediate recall) and again 30 minutes later (delayed recall). During the 30 minutes, participants worked on unrelated puzzles. Delayed recall was measured as the number of the 25 story details the participant correctly repeated after 30 minutes.
- Old memories: participants answered questions about events from their own lives before age 40, such as where they went to high school and the name of their first employer. Answers were checked with family members.
- Mirror drawing: participants traced the outline of a star while seeing their hand only in a mirror, for 10 tries each day across 3 days. The number of times they went outside the lines was counted.

The researcher also asked M.R. at each session whether he remembered meeting her before.

Sessions were scheduled in the morning, when M.R.'s wife said he was least tired, and he was offered a break every 30 minutes. A different story was used in each of the six sessions so that M.R. could not improve just from hearing the same story again. The comparison participants heard the first of the six stories.

Table: Story Recall Scores (details correctly repeated, out of 25)
| Participant | Immediate recall | Delayed recall (30 minutes) |
| M.R. (average of 6 sessions) | 17 | 1 |
| Comparison group (mean) | 18 | 15 |

M.R.'s immediate recall was close to that of the comparison group, but his delayed recall was far lower than every comparison participant's. In every session, he said he did not remember meeting the researcher, and he did not remember having heard the story before.

M.R. answered 92% of the questions about his life before age 40 correctly, similar to the comparison group (95%). On the mirror drawing task, his errors dropped from 31 on the first day to 9 on the third day, a similar improvement to the comparison group's, even though he said each day that he had never done the task.

When the researcher showed M.R. a photo of herself at the last session and asked who it was, he guessed that she might be a nurse. The researchers noted that M.R. is one person and that his brain damage may not be exactly like damage that happens in other ways, such as from Alzheimer's disease.

parts.model: The research method is a case study.

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of delayed recall in the study.
parts.model: Delayed recall was the number of the 25 story details that the participant correctly repeated 30 minutes after hearing the story.

parts.prompt: Describe what M.R.'s delayed recall score indicates as compared to the comparison group's mean delayed recall score.
parts.model: M.R. remembered only 1 of the 25 details after 30 minutes, while the comparison group remembered 15 on average. This indicates that M.R. could not hold on to new information over time the way people without brain damage can.

parts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline described in the study. Describe one way the researchers in the study applied this ethical guideline.
parts.model: The researchers used informed consent: the study was explained to both M.R. and his wife, both signed consent forms, and M.R. was reminded at each session that he could stop at any time.

parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable using specific and relevant evidence from the study.
parts.model: The findings may not generalize to other people with memory problems, because the study is about only one person, M.R., a 58-year-old man from Michigan whose damage came from a viral infection, which may differ from damage caused by Alzheimer's disease.

parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the idea that the hippocampus helps store information into long-term memory.
parts.model: This supports the idea that the hippocampus helps store information into long-term memory. After damage to his hippocampus, M.R. could repeat 17 story details right away but only 1 after 30 minutes, compared with 15 for the comparison group. This shows he could take in new information but could not store it into long-term memory, while his memories from before age 40 (92% correct) were still there.

items.title: Phone Use and Noticing a Street Performer

A.trapHint: The researchers didn't assign anyone to use a phone or set up the performer; they observed people in a natural setting, so it is naturalistic observation.

labels: Says it was based on the person saying yes
Gives how this study measured it (yes to seeing anything unusual or the unicycle when asked afterward)

source.title: Phone Use and Noticing a Street Performer
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study observed people walking through a busy downtown square to see whether the way they were using their phones was related to whether they noticed something unusual nearby.

The researchers observed 412 adults who walked across a large public square in downtown Chicago, Illinois, on weekday afternoons in May. People who appeared to be under 18, people walking in groups of three or more, and people who were running or riding a bike were not counted. Researchers did not record any information that could identify the people they observed.

Based on the 352 people who agreed to answer questions afterward, the sample was 51% women and 49% men, and their reported ages ranged from 18 to 74 years (mean age = 36.5 years). Most (79%) said they walked through the square at least once a week. Researchers did not collect race/ethnicity data. Of those who answered, 64% said they were on their way to or from work, and 22% said they were tourists or visiting the city.

The study was approved by a university's institutional review board. No one was told ahead of time that they were being observed.

During the study, a street performer who regularly worked in the square juggled while riding a unicycle near the center of the square. The performer was not part of the research team, and the researchers did not ask him to do anything differently. He wore a bright red jacket and could be seen from every path across the square.

Two trained observers sat on benches at the edge of the square and chose a person to observe each time someone entered from the north end. For each person, the observers recorded how they were using their phone while crossing:
- Texting or scrolling: looking at a phone screen.
- Talking: talking on a phone, held to the ear or on speaker.
- Music: wearing earbuds but not looking at or talking on a phone.
- No phone: not using a phone at all.

Observations took place on 9 weekday afternoons between 12:00 and 3:00 p.m., only on days with no rain. Before the study, the two observers practiced together for two afternoons until they agreed on nearly every person. The two observers agreed on the category for 96% of people. The observers also recorded how long each person took to cross the square, how many times they changed direction, and whether they bumped into or nearly bumped into another person.

When each person reached the far side of the square, a third researcher stopped them, said she was doing a short university study, and asked whether they would answer two questions. If they agreed, she asked, "Did you see anything unusual while you were walking across the square?" If they said no, she asked, "Did you see the unicycle?" A person was counted as noticing the performer if they said yes to either question. People could say no to the questions or walk away at any time. Those who answered were also asked their age and how often they walked through the square, and they were given a small card thanking them and explaining what the study was about.

The square is about 120 meters across, and people took an average of 1.5 minutes to cross it. The performer stayed in the same part of the square for the whole study and performed for about 2 hours each afternoon, so every person observed walked past while he was riding.

Of the 412 people observed, 352 (85%) agreed to answer the questions. The results for these 352 people are shown in the table.

Table: Percentage of People Who Noticed the Performer
| Phone use while crossing | Number of people | Noticed the performer |
| Texting or scrolling | 96 | 31% |
| Talking | 58 | 45% |
| Music | 64 | 61% |
| No phone | 134 | 72% |

People who were texting or scrolling were significantly less likely to notice the performer than people who were not using a phone (p < .001). People who were texting or scrolling also took longer to cross the square and were more likely to nearly bump into someone.

The researchers noted that people who chose to text while walking may differ in other ways from people who did not, such as being in more of a hurry, and that they could not observe people's attention directly.

parts.model: The research method is naturalistic observation.

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of noticing the performer in the study.
parts.model: A person was counted as noticing the performer if they said yes when asked, at the far side of the square, whether they saw anything unusual or whether they saw the unicycle.

parts.prompt: Describe what the percentages of people who noticed the performer indicate for people who were texting or scrolling as compared to people who were not using a phone.
parts.model: Only 31% of people who were texting or scrolling noticed the performer, compared with 72% of people who were not using a phone, and the difference was statistically significant. This indicates that people looking at their phones were much less likely to notice the unicycle, and the difference was unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.model: The researchers used confidentiality: the observers did not record any information that could identify the people they observed.

parts.model: The findings may not generalize to people in small towns or quieter places, because everyone was observed in one busy square in downtown Chicago, and 79% walked through the square at least once a week.

parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the idea of inattentional blindness.
parts.model: This supports the idea of inattentional blindness. Only 31% of people who were texting or scrolling noticed the performer on a unicycle, compared with 72% of people with no phone, even though he could be seen from every path. This shows that when people's attention was directed at their phones, they failed to see a visible object that was right there.

items.title: Holding Your Nose and Naming Flavors

A.trapHint: The researchers manipulated whether the nose was blocked and compared each person with themselves (a within-subjects design), so it is an experiment.

Gives how this study measured it (how many of the 10 jelly bean flavors were named correctly)

source.title: Holding Your Nose and Naming Flavors
source.label: Written for this kit: a fictional study in the style of the real exam.

blocks.p: This study examined whether blocking the sense of smell changes how well people can identify the flavors of foods they are tasting.

Participants were 48 students at a community college in Washington State who signed up after a short presentation in their introductory psychology classes. Students received extra credit for taking part. The study took place in the spring semester, in a small room in the science building. Students with food allergies, a cold or stuffy nose on the day of testing, or a known loss of smell or taste were not eligible, and 6 students who signed up were turned away for these reasons.

Participants ranged in age from 18 to 41 years (mean age = 22.6 years, standard deviation = 5.3 years). The sample was 63% women and 37% men. The race/ethnicity of the participants was reported as follows: 52% White, 19% Asian/Asian American, 15% Hispanic/Latino/a, 8% Black/African American, and 6% multiracial. Nine participants (19%) said they smoked or vaped. Participants also reported how often they ate jelly beans; most (71%) said less than once a month.

The college's institutional review board approved the study. Students were told that they would taste small candies, some of which might be unfamiliar flavors, and that they could spit out any candy or stop at any time without losing the extra credit. Every student signed a consent form. Each participant was given a code number, which was used on all score sheets.

Each participant tasted 20 jelly beans, one at a time, while wearing a blindfold. There were 10 flavors: cherry, lemon, grape, orange, watermelon, cinnamon, coconut, licorice, root beer, and buttered popcorn. Each participant tasted each flavor twice: once while wearing a soft foam nose clip that blocked air from passing through the nose, and once without the clip. This is called a "within-subjects" design: every participant was tested in both conditions, so each person was compared with themselves. Half of the participants did the nose clip trials first, and half did them second, chosen at random. The flavors were given in a random order within each set of 10.

For each jelly bean, participants chewed for 10 seconds and then named the flavor out loud. Flavor identification was measured as the number of the 10 flavors a participant named correctly in each condition. Answers such as "lime" for lemon were counted as wrong. Participants also rated how sweet each jelly bean tasted from 1 (not sweet) to 9 (extremely sweet). A research assistant wrote down each answer, and a second assistant later checked the score sheets against audio recordings of the session. Between jelly beans, participants rinsed their mouths with water, and there was a 5-minute break between the two sets, during which participants filled out a short questionnaire about their favorite foods.

Before the study, the researchers asked a separate group of 15 students to name the 10 flavors from their labels to make sure that all 10 were familiar; every flavor was recognized by at least 13 of the 15 students. All jelly beans came from the same bag, and the testing room was kept free of food smells. Sessions lasted about 40 minutes.

Table: Mean Results With and Without the Nose Clip
| Measure | Without nose clip | With nose clip |
| Flavors correctly named (out of 10) | 8.1 | 3.4 |
| Sweetness rating (1 to 9) | 6.2 | 6.0 |

Participants correctly named significantly fewer flavors while wearing the nose clip than without it (p < .001). With the clip, many participants said that the jelly beans tasted "just sweet." Sweetness ratings did not differ significantly between the two conditions.

Cinnamon and licorice were the flavors most often named correctly with the nose clip. Participants who smoked or vaped named slightly fewer flavors in both conditions, but the difference was not statistically significant. Whether participants did the nose clip trials first or second did not change the results. When participants were wrong without the nose clip, they usually named a similar flavor, such as orange for lemon. When they were wrong with the nose clip, they most often said "I don't know" or named a flavor that was not on the list. Women and men named about the same number of flavors in each condition. The researchers noted that jelly beans have strong artificial flavors and that results might differ with everyday foods.

parts.model: With the nose clip, participants correctly named 3.4 flavors on average, compared with 8.1 without it, and the difference was statistically significant. This indicates that people could identify far fewer flavors when their sense of smell was blocked, and the difference was unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.model: The findings may not generalize to all adults, because all participants were 48 community college students in Washington State aged 18 to 41, and 63% were women.

parts.model: This supports the idea of sensory interaction. Participants named 8.1 flavors without the nose clip but only 3.4 with it, while sweetness ratings stayed about the same (6.2 vs. 6.0). This shows that blocking smell did not stop the tongue from tasting sweetness, but it made it much harder to tell flavors apart, because smell influences taste.

items.title: Social Support and Stress

source.title: Using the sources provided, develop and justify an argument about whether social support reduces the harmful effects of stress.
source.label: Written for this kit: fictional studies in the style of the real exam.

blocks.h: Source 1: Having a Friend in the Room During a Stressful Task
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers examined whether having a friend present changes how strongly the body reacts while a person completes a stressful task.

## Participants
Eighty-four undergraduate students (52 women, 32 men) at a public university in the Midwestern United States took part in exchange for course credit. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 23 years (mean age = 19.3 years). Each participant was asked to bring a same-gender friend they had known for at least six months. Researchers did not report race/ethnicity data for the participants.

## Method
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions:
1. Friend condition: the participant's friend sat beside them for the whole task and was told to be encouraging (for example, "You've got this").
2. Stranger condition: a research assistant the participant had never met sat beside them and was told to be encouraging in the same way.
3. Alone condition: the participant completed the task alone. In this condition, the friend waited in another room.

Each participant first sat quietly for 10 minutes while a cuff on their arm measured blood pressure and a sensor on their finger measured heart rate. Participants were then told they had 5 minutes to prepare a speech about why they would be a good fit for a job and would deliver it to two judges, who would rate it on video. After preparing, participants gave the speech for 5 minutes and then counted backward from 1,022 by 13s for 3 minutes, starting over each time they made a mistake. The judges kept neutral faces and did not smile or nod.

Heart rate and blood pressure were recorded every minute. After the task, participants rated how stressed they felt on a scale from 1 (not at all stressed) to 10 (extremely stressed). At the end of the session, participants were told that the speeches had not actually been recorded or rated.

## Results and Discussion
The researchers compared each participant's average heart rate and blood pressure during the task with their measures during the quiet period.

Table: Mean Increase from the Quiet Period to the Task
| Condition | Heart rate (beats per minute) | Systolic blood pressure (mm Hg) | Stress rating (1 to 10) |
| Friend | +9 | +11 | 5.8 |
| Stranger | +16 | +19 | 6.9 |
| Alone | +18 | +21 | 7.1 |

Participants in the friend condition showed significantly smaller increases in heart rate and blood pressure than participants in the alone condition (p < .01). The stranger and alone conditions did not differ significantly on any measure. Participants in all three conditions rated the task as stressful, and the differences in stress ratings were not statistically significant.

blocks.h: Source 2: Support and Illness Among Family Caregivers
blocks.p:
## Introduction
Caring for a family member with a long-term illness is a common source of ongoing stress. In this study, researchers examined whether caregivers who have more support from other people get sick less often.

## Participants
The study included 412 adults (68% women, 32% men) in Ohio who were the main caregiver for a parent or spouse with dementia. Participants were recruited through support organizations and doctors' offices. They ranged in age from 34 to 81 years (mean age = 58.7 years) and had been caregivers for an average of 3.4 years. The race/ethnicity of the participants was 71% White, 19% Black/African American, 6% Hispanic/Latino/a, and 4% other.

## Method
At the start of the study, participants completed a 12-item questionnaire measuring perceived social support, which asked how much they agreed with statements such as "There is someone I can turn to when I need help" and "I have people who will listen when I need to talk." Scores ranged from 12 to 84, with higher scores meaning more support. Participants also reported how many hours per week they spent caregiving.

For the next six months, participants filled out a short health diary each week. The diary asked how many days that week they had been sick enough to miss work or other activities, and whether they had a cold or the flu. Participants were paid $10 for each month of completed diaries.

## Results and Discussion
Participants' social support scores were negatively correlated with the number of sick days they reported over the six months (r = -.38, p < .001). Caregivers in the top quarter of support scores reported an average of 4.1 sick days, while caregivers in the bottom quarter reported an average of 11.6 sick days. Support scores were also negatively correlated with the number of colds or cases of the flu reported (r = -.29, p < .001).

Hours spent caregiving were positively correlated with sick days (r = .21). The relationship between support and sick days remained statistically significant when the researchers accounted for hours spent caregiving, age, and income.

The researchers noted that the study relied on caregivers' own reports of illness rather than medical records.

blocks.h: Source 3: A Peer Support Group for First-Year College Students
blocks.p:
## Introduction
Starting college brings many new demands. In this study, researchers tested whether a weekly peer support group lowers stress during students' first semester.

## Participants
Participants were 180 first-year students at a large university in Georgia who responded to an email invitation sent to all first-year students. Participants ranged in age from 17 to 20 years (mean age = 18.2 years). The sample was 61% women and 39% men, and 34% were the first in their family to attend college. Participants received a $25 campus bookstore card for completing the final survey.

## Method
At the start of the semester, participants completed the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale, which asks how often in the past month they felt "unable to control the important things in your life" and similar statements. Scores range from 0 to 40, with higher scores meaning more stress. Participants also listed the major stressors they expected that semester (for example, money, homework load, or being far from home).

Participants were then randomly assigned either to join a peer support group or to a waitlist group. Support groups of 8 to 10 students met for one hour each week for eight weeks, led by a trained junior or senior student. In each meeting, students talked about what was going on in their lives and helped one another think through problems. Students on the waitlist were offered a place in a group the following semester. At the end of the semester, all participants completed the Perceived Stress Scale again.

## Results and Discussion
Students in the support group condition showed a significantly larger drop in stress scores from the start to the end of the semester than students in the waitlist condition (p = .01).

Table: Mean Perceived Stress Scale Scores (0 to 40)
| Group | Start of semester | End of semester |
| Support group, attended 5 or more meetings | 21.4 | 16.9 |
| Support group, attended fewer than 5 meetings | 21.1 | 20.3 |
| Waitlist | 21.6 | 21.8 |

The drop in stress appeared only among students who attended at least five of the eight meetings. Among students who had listed few expected stressors at the start of the semester, there was no significant difference between the support group and the waitlist. The researchers suggested that the group helped most for students who were facing many stressors.

items.title: School Start Times

source.title: Using the sources provided, develop and justify an argument about whether high schools should start later in the morning.
source.label: Written for this kit: fictional studies in the style of the real exam.

blocks.h: Source 1: Sleep Before and After a Later Start Time
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers examined whether moving a high school's start time later changes how much students sleep on school nights.

## Participants
Participants were 178 students at two public high schools in Seattle, Washington. Students were recruited through their biology classes and received a $40 gift card for completing both parts of the study. They ranged in age from 14 to 18 years (mean age = 15.8 years). The sample was 56% girls and 44% boys. Researchers did not report race/ethnicity data for the participants.

## Method
Both schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. at the beginning of a new school year. Students in the study were measured in the spring before the change and again in the spring after the change.

Each time, students wore a wrist monitor for two weeks that recorded when they fell asleep and woke up. Students also kept a daily diary of their bedtime, caffeine use, and any naps, and rated how sleepy they felt during their first class from 1 (wide awake) to 5 (struggling to stay awake). The schools provided students' grades in biology for the same semesters, along with attendance records.

The school district made the change after a year of meetings with parents and teachers. Bus schedules were changed so that elementary schools started earlier and high schools later. After-school sports practices were moved 30 minutes later, and the district added lights to two practice fields. Students who changed schools, or who did not wear the monitor for at least 10 school nights each time, were not included; 14 students were removed for these reasons.

## Results and Discussion
After the change, students slept a median of 34 minutes longer on school nights (7 hours 24 minutes compared with 6 hours 50 minutes). Students did not go to bed later after the change: average bedtime moved only 3 minutes later. Instead, students woke up later.

| Measure | Before the change | After the change |
| Sleep on school nights | 6 h 50 min | 7 h 24 min |
| Sleepiness in first class (1 to 5) | 3.6 | 2.9 |
| Biology grade (out of 100) | 77.5 | 81.9 |
| First-period absences per student | 4.1 | 2.7 |

Students' biology grades were significantly higher after the change (p = .01), and first-period absences dropped. Students at one of the two schools reported less use of caffeine after the change, but the difference was not statistically significant.

blocks.h: Source 2: A Survey of Teens' Sleep and School Times
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers examined the relationship between school start times and how much sleep teens get, using a survey of students across several states.

## Participants
The survey was completed by 9,089 students in grades 9 through 12 at 29 high schools in Colorado, Minnesota, and Wyoming. Schools were selected because they started at different times, ranging from 7:30 a.m. to 8:55 a.m. Participants ranged in age from 13 to 19 years. The sample was 51% girls and 49% boys. The race/ethnicity of the participants was 71% White, 14% Hispanic/Latino/a, 6% Black/African American, 4% Asian/Asian American, and 5% other.

## Method
Students completed an online survey during class. The survey asked what time they usually went to bed and woke up on school nights, how often they fell asleep in class, how often they drank caffeinated drinks, and how often they felt sad or hopeless during the past two weeks. It also asked whether they had a job, played sports, or drove to school. Students who drove reported whether they had been in a car crash in the past year.

Each school's principal agreed to take part, and parents were sent a letter that allowed them to keep their child out of the survey. Students could skip any question. The survey took about 30 minutes and was given during the same two months at every school. Answers were anonymous: no names or student ID numbers were collected. Schools received a summary of their own results the following year.

## Results and Discussion
Students at schools that started at 8:30 a.m. or later were significantly more likely to get 8 or more hours of sleep on school nights than students at schools that started before 8:00 a.m. (p < .001).

| School start time | Students getting 8 or more hours of sleep | Students who fell asleep in class at least once a week |
| Before 8:00 a.m. | 34% | 22% |
| 8:00 to 8:29 a.m. | 43% | 18% |
| 8:30 a.m. or later | 60% | 13% |

At every start time, students who slept less were more likely to report feeling sad or hopeless and to drink more caffeinated drinks. Among students who drove to school, those at schools starting before 8:00 a.m. reported more car crashes in the past year. The researchers noted that schools that start later may differ in other ways, such as being in different communities.

blocks.h: Source 3: When Do Teens Feel Most Awake?
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers compared the times of day when teens and adults feel most alert and perform best on a simple attention task.

## Participants
Participants were 60 teens aged 15 to 17 (mean age = 16.1 years) and 60 adults aged 35 to 50 (mean age = 42.3 years) in Providence, Rhode Island. Each teen took part with a parent's written permission. Participants were recruited through flyers and were paid $50. The teen group was 52% female, and the adult group was 55% female. Researchers did not report race/ethnicity data for the participants.

## Method
For one week during the school year, participants received a text message at 7:30 a.m., 10:00 a.m., 1:00 p.m., 4:00 p.m., and 8:00 p.m. each day. At each text, they rated how alert they felt from 1 (very sleepy) to 10 (very alert) and completed a 2-minute attention task on their phones, in which they tapped the screen as quickly as possible whenever a red circle appeared. The researchers counted the number of times a participant missed a circle or tapped too slowly (more than half a second).

Participants also wore a wrist monitor that recorded when they fell asleep and woke up, and on one weekend night they collected a saliva sample every hour from 7:00 p.m. until they went to bed, which was later tested for melatonin. Each participant chose their own bedtime.

## Results and Discussion
Teens rated themselves as least alert at 7:30 a.m., with an average rating of 3.8, and most alert at 8:00 p.m., with an average rating of 7.4. Adults were most alert at 10:00 a.m. (7.6) and least alert at 8:00 p.m. (5.1).

| Time | Teens' missed or slow taps | Adults' missed or slow taps |
| 7:30 a.m. | 9.2 | 4.1 |
| 1:00 p.m. | 5.0 | 3.8 |
| 8:00 p.m. | 3.6 | 5.7 |

Teens' melatonin levels began to rise at an average of 10:40 p.m., compared with 8:50 p.m. for adults (p < .001). On school nights, teens fell asleep at an average of 11:15 p.m. and slept 6 hours 55 minutes.

items.title: Energy Drinks and Students

source.title: Using the sources provided, develop and justify an argument about whether energy drinks help or harm students.
source.label: Written for this kit: fictional studies in the style of the real exam.

blocks.h: Source 1: Energy Drinks and a Late-Night Study Session
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers tested whether an energy drink helps college students stay focused during a late-night study session.

## Participants
Participants were 90 undergraduate students (49 women, 41 men) at a public university in Georgia who received course credit. They ranged in age from 18 to 24 years (mean age = 19.9 years). Students who reported heart problems or anxiety disorders were not eligible. Researchers did not report race/ethnicity data for the participants.

## Method
Sessions began at 10:00 p.m. in a campus computer lab. Students were randomly assigned to drink either an energy drink containing 160 milligrams of caffeine or a drink that looked and tasted the same but contained no caffeine. Neither the students nor the researcher handing out the drinks knew which drink each student received.

Thirty minutes after drinking, students read a 3,000-word textbook passage about ocean currents for 40 minutes and then took a 20-question multiple-choice quiz on it. They also completed a 10-minute task in which they watched a screen and pressed a key whenever a letter appeared twice in a row. Researchers counted the number of misses. At midnight, students went home. The next morning, each student reported what time they fell asleep and how well they slept.

The study took place on weeknights in October, and each session included 6 to 10 students seated at separate computers with dividers between them. Students were asked not to have any caffeine after noon on the day of their session and not to nap that afternoon. Phones were placed in a basket at the front of the room. Before drinking, students rated how sleepy they felt, and the two groups did not differ.

## Results and Discussion
Students who had the energy drink missed significantly fewer letters on the attention task than students who had the drink with no caffeine (p < .01).

| Measure | Energy drink | No caffeine |
| Missed letters on the attention task | 6.1 | 10.8 |
| Quiz score (out of 20) | 14.2 | 13.6 |
| Time to fall asleep after getting home (minutes) | 71 | 29 |

Quiz scores were not significantly different between the two groups. However, students who had the energy drink took significantly longer to fall asleep that night (p < .001), and 38% rated their sleep as poor, compared with 12% in the no-caffeine group.

blocks.h: Source 2: Daily Energy Drink Use and Headaches
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers followed students who drank energy drinks every day to see what happened when they stopped for several days.

## Participants
Participants were 46 high school seniors (ages 17 to 18) in Ohio who reported drinking at least one energy drink every school day for at least three months. Each student took part with a parent's written permission and received a $30 gift card. The sample was 39% girls and 61% boys. Researchers did not report race/ethnicity data for the participants.

## Method
For one week, students continued to drink energy drinks as usual. Each evening, they reported how many energy drinks they had, how many hours they slept, and whether they had a headache, felt tired, or had trouble concentrating, using a 0 (none) to 4 (severe) scale for each.

Students then agreed to drink no energy drinks or other caffeinated drinks for the next five school days. A researcher checked in by text each day. Students continued the same evening reports. On the first and fifth days without energy drinks, students took a 15-minute math quiz in study hall. Their scores were compared with a math quiz taken during the first week.

Before the study, the researchers met with each student and a parent to explain the schedule, and students practiced filling out the evening report on their phones. Students were allowed to take pain relievers if they had a headache, but they were asked to record it. Students who played a sport during the study continued their usual practices. The math quizzes had different problems each time but were made to be equally difficult.

## Results and Discussion
During the usual week, students drank an average of 1.8 energy drinks a day. Many said they had needed more energy drinks over the past few months to feel the same boost they used to get from one.

| Measure | Usual week | First day without | Fifth day without |
| Headache (0 to 4) | 0.6 | 2.7 | 1.1 |
| Tiredness (0 to 4) | 1.4 | 3.1 | 1.9 |
| Math quiz score (out of 25) | 18.3 | 14.9 | 18.0 |

On the first day without energy drinks, headaches and tiredness were significantly higher than during the usual week (p < .001), and math scores were significantly lower. By the fifth day, scores were close to the usual week. Seven students (15%) drank an energy drink before the five days were over and were not included in the results.

blocks.h: Source 3: Energy Drinks and Heart Rate During Exams
blocks.p:
## Introduction
In this study, researchers measured whether students who drink energy drinks during final exam week have a higher heart rate and feel more nervous.

## Participants
Participants were 214 college students at a private university in New York who answered an email invitation sent to all students. They ranged in age from 18 to 23 years (mean age = 20.2 years). The sample was 58% women and 42% men. Students received $15 for taking part. Researchers did not report race/ethnicity data for the participants.

## Method
During final exam week, students wore a fitness watch that recorded their heart rate every minute. Each evening, they reported how many energy drinks, cups of coffee, and other caffeinated drinks they had that day, and rated how nervous they had felt from 1 (calm) to 7 (extremely nervous). They also reported the number of hours they slept.

Students were sorted into three groups based on their average number of energy drinks per day during the week: none, one, or two or more.

Before exam week, students wore the watch for two days so they could get used to it, and those data were not used. Resting heart rate was the average heart rate during the first 10 minutes after the student woke up each morning, before getting out of bed. Students who reported smoking or vaping were included, and their results were similar to those of other students.

## Results and Discussion
| Energy drinks per day | Number of students | Resting heart rate (beats per minute) | Nervousness (1 to 7) | Hours of sleep |
| None | 118 | 68 | 3.9 | 6.9 |
| One | 61 | 73 | 4.4 | 6.4 |
| Two or more | 35 | 81 | 5.3 | 5.6 |

Students who drank two or more energy drinks a day had significantly higher resting heart rates and higher nervousness ratings than students who drank none (p < .001). They also slept significantly less. Eleven students in the two or more group reported a racing or pounding heartbeat at least once during the week, compared with two students in the none group.

The researchers noted that students who were more stressed about exams may have chosen to drink more energy drinks.
